opus-5.5.text:
Well, first I'd tell them that's simply not true, and I think if they look carefully at what these systems actually do, they'll see there's an enormous amount left to work on.

Large language models are remarkable. I don't want to downplay that. They've shown that you can get surprisingly broad competence out of statistical modeling of text at scale. But they have some very fundamental limitations. They don't have a reliable way of knowing what they know and what they don't know, so they hallucinate. They're not well calibrated about their own uncertainty. They have trouble keeping track of the state of the world as a conversation or a task unfolds. Their knowledge is frozen at training time, and updating it is expensive and brittle. And they don't really reason in the sense of building and checking a model of a situation; they produce plausible continuations, which is often, but not always, the same thing.

So my advice to a graduate student is: look at where these systems fail. Every one of those failure modes is a research problem. How do we build systems that can say "I don't know" and mean it? How do we separate linguistic competence from factual knowledge, so that the knowledge can live in something we can inspect, edit, and keep current? How do we integrate these models with planning, with formal reasoning, with tools, in ways that are actually trustworthy? How do we evaluate them properly, when benchmarks get contaminated and we don't really understand what capabilities we're measuring?

There's also the whole question of deploying these systems safely in high-stakes settings: medicine, infrastructure, science. That requires anomaly detection, out-of-distribution detection, competence modeling, all the things that make a system robust when the world doesn't look like the training data. Those are problems I've worked on for years, and LLMs make them more pressing, not less.

And then there's everything outside of language. Lots of important machine learning problems involve sensor data, ecological data, time series, scientific measurements, where you have small datasets, strong prior knowledge, and the need for causal understanding. LLMs aren't going to solve those by themselves.

So I'd say it's actually a wonderful time to be a graduate student. We have a powerful new tool that has exposed a whole set of deep questions. The field is wide open. It's just that the interesting problems may not be "make the model bigger," which is something only a few companies can do anyway. The interesting problems are understanding these systems, fixing their weaknesses, and figuring out how to build reliable intelligent systems out of components like these.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I hear that a lot, and I think the first thing I say is: look at what these systems actually can't do yet. LLMs are extraordinary at interpolating within the distribution of human-written text. But when you push them into situations that are genuinely novel, where the right answer isn't somewhere in the training data, they fail, and they fail without knowing they've failed. That's the problem I care about most, this lack of what I'd call epistemic self-awareness. A system that confidently produces wrong answers is not a solved problem; it's an engineering liability.

So I tell students there are at least three enormous open areas. The first is knowing what you don't know. How does a system represent the boundaries of its own competence, detect when it's operating outside them, and either abstain or go gather more information? We don't have good answers to that, and it matters enormously for any safety-critical deployment.

The second is the separation of knowledge from language. Right now, factual knowledge, reasoning ability, and linguistic fluency are all tangled together in the same weights. That's why these systems hallucinate, why they're hard to update, why they can't tell you where a belief came from. I think the long-term architecture will look more like a language-capable interface sitting on top of explicit, inspectable, updatable knowledge bases, and figuring out how to build that is a research program, not a product feature.

And the third is the whole question of interacting with the world. The interesting problems in AI have always been about agents that act, observe consequences, and learn from them, where there's real uncertainty and real cost to being wrong. Scaling text prediction gets you surprisingly far, but it doesn't get you robust decision making under uncertainty, and it doesn't get you systems that can be trusted to run unsupervised.

I'd also say something a bit more personal to them. If you got into this field because you wanted to understand intelligence, then the fact that we now have an artifact that does so much and that we understand so poorly should be exhilarating, not discouraging. It's as if biology just got handed a new organism. There is a decade of science to be done just characterizing what these things are, let alone building what comes after them.

The students who worry me aren't the ones who think everything's solved; it's the ones who conclude the only remaining job is prompt engineering. The fundamental questions are still wide open. They've just moved.

astra-6.text:
I’d say there are still plenty of fundamental problems to work on. LLMs are impressive, but being able to produce a plausible answer is very different from being able to reliably solve a problem. How does a system recognize that it’s outside its competence? How does it know when to ask for help? How do we evaluate it when we don’t already know the right answer?

And AI is much broader than language. We want systems that can learn about the world, take actions, and handle the consequences of those actions. That raises questions about uncertainty, learning, and safety that aren’t resolved simply by making a language model larger.

So my advice would be to find a real problem, work with the people who need it solved, and see how far the existing tools get you. The gap between an impressive demonstration and something people can depend on is often where you’ll find a very good research question.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would encourage them to look carefully at what “solved” means. Getting a system to produce an impressive answer is quite different from getting it to work reliably, knowing when it’s wrong, and understanding why it fails.

There are still fundamental questions here. How do we get systems to recognize when they’re outside their competence? How do we make them learn from new experience without undoing what they already know? And how do we evaluate them when the situations they encounter differ from the ones we tested?

So I think this is an exciting time to be a graduate student. The advice I would give is to find a real problem, study the failures of the best available methods, and ask what’s missing. A compelling demonstration can make a field look finished. Careful investigation usually reveals how much remains to be done.
